newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope urges Albanians to lay down their weapons.
newsitem.headline: Pope urges Albanians to lay down their weapons.

text.p: Pope John Paul, who once hailed the bloodless collapse of communist rule in Albania as a miracle, urged Albanians on Sunday to end "destructive violence" and lay down their arms.

He said Europe had a duty to help rebuild the shattered Balkan country, where more than 100 people have been killed as violence sparked by the collapse of shady savings schemes has turned into a lawless revolt against President Sali Berisha.

"For the good of Albania, I urge all those who have taken up arms to lay them down. Destructive violence is definitely not the right way to resolve social problems," the Pontiff said in a regular weekly address to pilgrims in St Peter's Square.

"These tragic events are a call to the whole of Europe -- it must help the leaders and the Albanian people to build their country on the basis of democracy and political and social dialogue," he said.
Civilians last week emptied arms depots vacated by demoralised soldiers and gun law has prevailed across much of the country as police disappeared from the streets.
Most of those killed were hit by falling bullets in several days of almost continuous random firing.
From the start of his papacy in 1978, the Pontiff spoke out against totalitarianism and persecution under Albania's late Stalinist dictator Enver Hoxha.
He finally visited Albania in 1993, three years after the restoration of religious freedom and the collapse of Europe's last hard-line communist regime.
Hoxha had banned religion and made Albania the world's first officially atheist state in 1967.

The Pontiff said in a mass during that trip that Albania, which Hoxha had tried to isolate during his 40-year rule, "had fallen deep into an abyss and it is truly a miracle that it was able to climb out without bloodshed".

Echoing the passion of his visit, the Pope said on Sunday that Albania had recently emerged from a "long period of inhuman dictatorship" and the latest crisis had plunged its people into total insecurity.
Thousands of Albanians have been scrambling on board a ramshackle flotilla of ships to cross the Adriatic sea and seek sanctuary in Italy.

The Pope urged pilgrims to pray for peace and said trust in the authorities, whom Albanians blame for the failure of the "get-rich-quick" saving schemes in Europe's poorest state, needed to be re-established.
"That cannot be achieved without public order," he said.
The European Union agreed on Sunday to send military and police advisers to Albania in a bid to help restore order.
EU foreign ministers meeting informally in the central Dutch countryside also agreed to consider providing protection for this mission if necessary, but stressed this was not a military operation.
"Any interventionist approach is off the table," one German diplomatic source said.
